newsitem.title: UK: Old trends are currency market's New Year friends.
newsitem.headline: Old trends are currency market's New Year friends.

text.p: Currency markets have greeted the New Year by continuing the key trends of the old year, buying sterling and selling yen and Swiss francs.
But while the trend will remain the market's friend for now, players should brace for turnarounds later in 1997, analysts said on Thursday.

"It would be tempting to assume that these trends can persist for some while yet...however, we do not feel that fundamental forces are conducive to a significant extension of these old themes," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

Soft-toned Japanese economic data, plus concerns over Japan's financial system and equity prices, have conspired to depress the yen. It hit 116.40 per dollar in Europe on December 31, its worst level since April 1993. Sterling scored a high of 198.80 yen on the last day of 1996, its strongest in more than four years, while mark/yen is seen preparing to break above its recent 45-month peak of 75.90.

"I don't think we've seen the top (in dollar/yen), there's more of this to come, but the turning point will probably occur some time during the second quarter when we get evidence coming through of Japanese economic recovery and U.S. slowdown," said Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets.

The yen will find ever-growing support as Japan's trade surplus -- especially with the U.S. -- rises again, while both Japanese and U.S. authorities will be reluctant to see the yen cheapen further, market watchers said.
"Put simply, the two factors which drove the yen into decline are no longer in operation," said Meggyesi.
The Swiss franc is also likely to encounter continued selling pressure in the near future as Switzerland's economy remains mired in recession, analysts believed.
The Swiss franc's recent low of 1.3536 per dollar was its softest level since July 1994, while it hit 87.20 centimes per mark on Tuesday -- its weakest in more than three years.
But farther out the franc should draw support from a pick-up in growth by the end of 1996, as well as from safe-haven moves as momentum towards European monetary union grows, some said.
While the yen and Swiss franc buckle under pressure, further undermined by their host countries' rock-bottom interest rates, sterling goes from strength to strength.

The market is banking on a near-term hike in UK interest rates, with speculation hotting up ahead of the next monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George on January 15.
Analysts are split on the outcome of that meeting, but those who see no January tightening still feel that a hike ahead of the looming UK general election is just a matter of time.

"It's quite difficult to see sterling reversing," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ. "We may see some sell-off if the Chancellor holds firm against the governor, but all the signs are that we're going to see higher UK interest rates this year."

But the pound may wobble as the election, which must be held by May, looms ever larger. Though the market appears largely comfortable with the prospect that opinion-poll favourite Labour will oust the ruling Conservative party, the political uncertainty will do sterling no favours, analysts warned.
And some question whether the fact that UK rates are on a different track from those in the rest of Europe is enough to justify such relentless appreciation in the exchange rate.
"The interest rate market is, if anything, still scaling back its interest rate forecasts," said DMG's Meggyesi. "So long as this is the case we remain wary about extending sterling exposure."
